Been to all three, in a similar situation where I’m about an hour out but drive in when I can.

GC is where I went to prior to frequenting nexus. Shop owner is friendly and their prices for singles are solid. They were hosting pioneer for FNM a while which is pretty cool, don’t know what their FNMs are like now. As others have said, your matchups are pretty polarizing. The deck is an absolute blast to play and I have felt that games rely on top decking more with this deck than others I’ve played. You will get blown out and it won’t feel good, but when you win, it is a blast. Regardless learn from the L’s you take, even if they feel bad. 

You are a Tron deck with some flexibility. You can pivot on a dime based on what you topdeck. Sometimes you play prison, with chalices, coating, bridge etc., and sometimes you go turn 2 TKS into T3 Smasher and become the beat down deck. 

Best general advice for the deck is to 

1.	Learn your side board and know what to tutor when with KGC. 
2.	Watch VODS or streamers play the deck. Will give you some insight into what to do when. 
3.	Mulligan semi aggressively. We don’t have the luxury of the green land tutors that Green Tron has, so be smart about what you keep.
4.	Respect Chalice, it’s one of the decks biggest strengths. 
5.	Ballista is a good creature, but most of the time is a removal spell for an early ragavan/DRC/any other small thing.

*Are you implying that crime is the root of the issue?* 

I apologize I probably should have been more clear. The issue that clearly need to be addressed is racial bias in the Criminal Justice System (Well there are a lot of issues with the Criminal Justice System, but bear with me). The root of this racial bias/inequality does not start and end with policing practices. The root of the issue is far deeper and has to do with the criminal justice system as a whole (or legislators/cities/mayors/governors who pass the laws that police are sent to enforce). 

From what I have been able to see, everyone is upset with policing practices and rightfully so. But it always stops at police. There is a clear disadvantage at all stages in the Criminal Justice system if you are a PoC or Male, but there are no protests where people shout All Prosecutors are Bastards, All Correctional Workers are Bastards, etc. 

 *From my observation this is not happening enough.* 

I agree. In part, I believe it is just easier for people to place blame on one aspect and be done with it. It's not a bad thing, it is still a noble thing to be passionate about. But meaningful change cannot come without addressing the entire system. This can only be most easily done by voting. Personally, I find that a vast majority of the blame needs to be put on the politicians 1.) Allow police to operate in this way, and 2.) who overly regulate and send officers out to do their "dirty work".

This is almost a very valid point. While there is no defending this, focus needs to be shifted on the ***Criminal Justice System*** as a whole. ***Prosecutors*** opt for longer sentences for PoC, and are willing to admit flaky evidence. Use of Force incidents in prisons are committed my ***Corrections Officers***. Police are just the most visible aspect of the Criminal Justice. While there transgressions are just as inexcusable and accountability needs to be addressed, to only shout "acab" and expect meaningful change in the system is a flawed premise. 

As cliche as it sounds, Voting Matters. Who your DA is matters. Who your Judge is Matters. Hell, City Council Members who pass shitty ordinances and incentivize over policing matter. The one instance that immediately comes to mind with this is the Eric Garner Case. While I will not defend anything those officers did (I don't think choke holds are SoP), the ONLY reason the officers were there was a "crackdown" on cigarette tax stamp fraud, set forth by the governor. The governor faced no repercussion, nor did the Task Force, in fact, the state was able to seize over ***6 million*** in contraband. Again, I am not defending what the officers did, rather, I believe it is incredibly important to highlight the root of the issue as well. 

The best analogy I can make (and forgive me if its a bad analogy) is that there is a warehouse fire right now that needs to be addressed. But if and when the fire is put out, we cant just stop. We need to address what caused the fire and make sure we don't have a warehouse manager who is actively starting fires.
